@@@ USER
I am new to Git. How do I start tracking a project, make my first commit, and see what changed? Show the commands and what I should see.
@@@ ASSISTANT
Do the one-time setup first, then the four commands you will use all day: `status`, `add`, `commit`, `log`.

**One-time setup** (your name appears on every commit):

```
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
```

**Start a project:**

```
cd my-project
git init
```

Git answers `Initialized empty Git repository in <path>/.git/`. A hidden `.git` folder now holds the whole history. Never edit it by hand, and never delete it unless you want to lose the history.

**Check, stage, commit:**

```
echo hello > notes.txt
git status
```

```
On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
	notes.txt

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)
```

```
git add notes.txt
git status -s
```

```
A  notes.txt
```

```
git commit -m "Add notes"
```

```
[main (root-commit) <hash>] Add notes
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 notes.txt
```

**See what changed later:**

```
echo "line two" >> notes.txt
git status -s
git diff
```

```
 M notes.txt
```

```
--- a/notes.txt
+++ b/notes.txt
@@ -1 +1,2 @@
 hello
+line two
```

**The idea behind it:** your files live in three places. The **working folder** (what you edit), the **staging area** (what will go into the next commit, filled by `git add`), and the **history** (made by `git commit`). Staging lets you commit only part of your work, so each commit tells one clear story.

Short status codes: `??` new file Git does not know yet, `A` added (staged), `M` modified (a space before `M` means not staged, a space after means staged), `UU` merge conflict.

Useful extras:
- `git log --oneline` shows the history, one line per commit.
- `git add -p` lets you stage only some parts of a file.
- `git commit -am "message"` stages and commits every **already tracked** file in one step (it does not add new files).
@@@ END

@@@ USER
I made a mistake in Git. How do I undo things: a change I do not want, a file I staged by accident, a wrong commit message, a bad commit, and untracked junk files?
@@@ ASSISTANT
The right command depends on **how far the mistake got**. Here they are from smallest to biggest. In the examples the history is `Add notes` followed by newer commits.

**1. Throw away changes in a file (not committed yet)**

```
git restore notes.txt
```

The file goes back to the last commit. **This cannot be undone**, because those edits were never saved in Git.

**2. Unstage a file (keep the edits)**

```
git add secret.txt
git restore --staged secret.txt
git status -s
```

```
?? secret.txt
```

**3. Fix the last commit message** (only if you have not pushed it):

```
git log --oneline
```

```
<hash> Add line tow
<hash> Add notes
```

```
git commit --amend -m "Add line two"
git log --oneline
```

```
<hash> Add line two
<hash> Add notes
```

The same trick adds a forgotten file to the last commit: `git add todo.txt` and then `git commit --amend --no-edit`. Amending creates a **new** commit (new hash), so do not amend commits other people already have.

**4. Undo a commit that is already shared: `revert`**

```
git revert --no-edit HEAD
git log --oneline
```

```
[main <hash>] Revert "Add buggy line"
<hash> Revert "Add buggy line"
<hash> Add buggy line
<hash> Add line two
<hash> Add notes
```

`revert` adds a **new commit that does the opposite**. History is kept, so it is safe for shared branches.

**5. Remove commits that only exist on your computer: `reset`**

```
git reset --hard HEAD~1
```

```
HEAD is now at <hash> Revert "Add buggy line"
```

- `--soft HEAD~2`: go back two commits but keep all the changes **staged**. Good for squashing small "wip" commits into one: afterwards run `git commit -m "Add a and b"`.
- `--mixed` (the default): the same, but the changes are not staged.
- `--hard`: also **deletes the changes** in your working folder.

**6. Rescue a commit you lost with reset: `reflog`**

```
git reflog
```

```
<hash> HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~1
<hash> HEAD@{1}: commit: Another bad commit
<hash> HEAD@{2}: revert: Revert "Add buggy line"
```

The reflog lists every place `HEAD` has been in the last weeks. To get the lost commit back: `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}`.

**7. Delete untracked junk files**

```
git clean -n
```

```
Would remove junk.txt
```

`-n` is a dry run that only **shows** what would be deleted. When the list is right, run `git clean -f`. Add `-d` to include folders.

Rules of thumb:
- Not committed: `restore`. Committed but not shared: `amend` or `reset`. Shared: `revert`.
- Before any `--hard` or `clean -f`, run `git status` and `git diff`. Those two commands delete work that nothing can bring back.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
I got "CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict" when I merged a branch. What does it mean and how do I fix it step by step?
@@@ ASSISTANT
A conflict means that **both branches changed the same lines**, and Git cannot know which version you want. Git stops in the middle of the merge and asks you to decide. Nothing is lost.

Here is a complete example. `main` changed `color: blue` to red, and the branch `feature/color` changed the same line to green.

```
git merge feature/color
```

```
Auto-merging config.txt
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in config.txt
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
```

```
git status -s
```

```
UU config.txt
```

`UU` means "both modified, unresolved". Open the file. Git marked the two versions:

```
title: My App
<<<<<<< HEAD
color: red
=======
color: green
>>>>>>> feature/color
size: 10
```

How to read it:
- Between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======` is **your current branch** (`main`).
- Between `=======` and `>>>>>>> feature/color` is **the branch you are merging in**.

**Steps:**
1. Edit the file so that it contains exactly what you want, and **delete the three marker lines** (`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`). You can keep one side, the other side, or a mix:

```
title: My App
color: green
size: 10
```

2. Mark it as solved and finish the merge:

```
git add config.txt
git commit -m "Merge feature/color, keep green"
```

3. Check the result and clean up the branch:

```
git log --oneline --graph
git branch -d feature/color
```

```
*   <hash> Merge feature/color, keep green
|\
| * <hash> Use green
* | <hash> Use red
|/
* <hash> Add config
```

```
Deleted branch feature/color (was <hash>).
```

Tips:
- To cancel the whole merge and go back to how things were: `git merge --abort`.
- Search for leftover markers before committing: `git diff --check` warns about them, or search the project for `<<<<<<<`.
- Conflicts are normal. You get fewer of them with small branches, merging `main` into your branch often, and not two people editing the same lines.
- Tools such as VS Code show the two sides with buttons "Accept Current / Accept Incoming / Accept Both". They do the same thing as the manual edit.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
How do I use git stash, and how do I stop Git from tracking files like .env or the target folder? I already committed .env by mistake.
@@@ ASSISTANT
**Stash: put unfinished work aside**

Use it when you must switch branches but your changes are not ready to commit.

```
git stash
git status -s
```

```
(nothing: the folder is clean again)
```

```
git stash list
```

```
stash@{0}: WIP on main: <hash> Merge feature/color, keep green
```

When you are back, bring the work back with `git stash pop` (it re-applies the changes and removes the stash). `git stash apply` re-applies but keeps the stash. By default new, untracked files are not stashed; add `-u` to include them.

**.gitignore: never track these files**

Write one pattern per line in a file called `.gitignore` in the project root:

```
target/
.env
node_modules/
*.log
```

Before the file exists, Git shows the files as new:

```
 M config.txt
?? .env
?? target/
```

After you create it, they disappear from `git status`, and only `.gitignore` shows up as new (`?? .gitignore`). Commit it so the whole team has the same rules:

```
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Add .gitignore"
```

**If a file is already tracked, .gitignore does not help.** It only affects untracked files. Remove it from Git **without deleting it from your disk**:

```
git rm --cached .env
git commit -m "Stop tracking .env"
git ls-files
```

```
.gitignore
config.txt
```

`.env` is no longer in the list, but the file still exists in your folder.

**Important for secrets:** a password, API key or token that was ever committed is still in the history and in every copy that was pushed. Removing the file is not enough. **Change the secret** (create a new key and disable the old one) first. Cleaning the history is a second step, and it is only useful after the secret is already invalid.

Good defaults to ignore: build output (`target/`, `dist/`, `build/`), dependencies (`node_modules/`, `.venv/`), secrets (`.env`), editor and system files (`.vscode/`, `.DS_Store`, `Thumbs.db`), and logs.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
Something in my project broke and I do not know which commit did it. How can I find the commit that changed a line, or the one that introduced a bug, in Git?
@@@ ASSISTANT
Git has three tools, from simple to powerful.

**1. `git blame`: who last changed each line, and in which commit**

```
git blame app.js
```

Every line is shown with the commit hash, author and date. Then `git show <hash>` shows that whole commit. In VS Code, the GitLens extension shows the same information next to each line.

**2. `git log -S`: when did this text appear or disappear?**

The file `app.js` had `let timeout = 30;`, and a later commit changed it to 5:

```
git log -S"timeout = 30" --oneline
```

```
<hash> Change timeout
<hash> Add timeout
```

It lists the commits where the number of occurrences of that text changed: the one that added it and the one that removed it. Other useful forms: `git log -p app.js` (every change to one file, with the diff) and `git log --oneline -- path/to/file`.

**3. `git bisect`: find the commit that broke something, automatically**

Bisect uses binary search: with 1000 commits it needs only about 10 tests. You give it a commit that is bad, a commit that was good, and a command that tells it which is which (exit code 0 = good, anything else = bad).

Example: the check script `check.sh` returns success only if `settings.txt` contains `price=10`. Commits 1 to 3 have it, commits 4 to 6 do not.

```
git log --oneline
```

```
<hash> Commit 6
<hash> Commit 5
<hash> Commit 4
<hash> Commit 3
<hash> Commit 2
<hash> Commit 1
```

```
git bisect start
git bisect bad HEAD
git bisect good <hash of Commit 1>
git bisect run ./check.sh
```

```
Bisecting: 2 revisions left to test after this (roughly 1 step)
running './check.sh'
running './check.sh'
running './check.sh'
<hash> is the first bad commit
```

Git prints the full details of that commit (author, date, message and files changed) after that line, and it says it was Commit 4. Finally, **always** go back to your normal branch:

```
git bisect reset
```

If you have no script, run `git bisect start`, then `git bisect bad` and `git bisect good <commit>`. Git checks out a commit in the middle; test your program by hand and type `git bisect good` or `git bisect bad`. Repeat until it names the first bad commit.

This works best when each commit is small and the project builds at every commit, which is another reason to commit often.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
How should I write good Git commit messages, and what is a sensible daily Git workflow for a small project when I work alone?
@@@ ASSISTANT
**A commit message has two parts:** a short subject line, then (only when needed) a blank line and a longer explanation.

```
Fix crash when the notes file is empty

The loader called unwrap() on the first line. An empty file has no
first line, so the program panicked. Return an empty list instead.
```

Rules that make history useful:
- **Subject: about 50 characters, no full stop, imperative mood.** Write "Add search box", not "Added search box" or "Adding search box". Test: it should finish the sentence "If applied, this commit will ...".
- **Say what and why, not how.** The diff already shows how. The body explains the reason, which nobody can read from the code later.
- **One idea per commit.** If you need the word "and" in the subject, it is probably two commits.
- Bad: `fix`, `update`, `changes`, `asdf`, `final2`. In three months nobody (including you) knows what they mean.

**A simple daily workflow for a solo project:**

1. Start from a clean, up to date `main`: `git status`, then `git pull` if you use a remote.
2. Make a branch for each task: `git switch -c feature/search`. Small branches are easy to merge and easy to throw away.
3. Work in small steps. When something works, commit it: `git add -p` (review what you stage), then `git commit`.
4. Look at what you are about to commit: `git diff --staged`. It catches debug prints and secrets.
5. Run your tests before the final commit.
6. Merge back: `git switch main`, `git merge feature/search`, then `git branch -d feature/search`.
7. Push to a remote (GitHub, GitLab) at the end of the day: `git push`. Your work is then safe even if your laptop breaks.

**Habits that save you:**
- Commit before big experiments, so you can always come back.
- Use `git status` all the time. It is free and tells you what to do next.
- Add a `.gitignore` in the first commit.
- Tag releases so you can find them later: `git tag v1.0.0` and `git push --tags`.
- Never commit passwords, keys or large generated files.
@@@ END
